title: Psychosocial and behavioral correlates of frailty, cognition, and allostatic load across nine years and within twin pairs
authors: Anqing Zheng, Deborah Finkel, Brian Karl Finch, Jenae M. Neiderhiser, and Chandra A. Reynolds
status: Companion to a manuscript under review.

home.question: Psychosocial and behavioral characteristics are routinely linked to aging one association at a time. This study examined how much they predict together.
home.lead: In the Midlife in the United States study (MIDUS), 161 psychosocial and behavioral characteristics added substantial prediction of current frailty and allostatic load, and a smaller increment for cognition, beyond 16 background characteristics and resources. Measured at midlife, they also predicted 9-year change in frailty and cognition beyond baseline status, explaining an additional 0.8% to 1.8% of variance, a meaningful increment given that baseline status already accounts for most of what is predictable. The allostatic-load increment was less stable.
home.closing: Joint prediction beyond current status, rather than the breadth of individual associations, offers a realistic benchmark for the prospective value of these characteristics.

design.label: Twin pairs
design.note: held out from frailty and cognition training

findings.title: Tier 2 predictors add substantial prediction of current frailty and allostatic load, and less for cognition
findings.lead: Beyond Tier 1 background variables, the Tier 2 block explained substantial additional variance in frailty and allostatic load and a more modest amount in cognition.
body: The Tier 2 increment was ΔR² = 37.9% for frailty, 11.6% for cognition, and 28.8% for allostatic load (full-model R² = 50.1%, 33.6%, and 33.0%; n = 5,410, 4,539, and 1,782).

Because the frailty index and some psychosocial measures may share self-report content, the frailty increment was recomputed after excluding the 29 Tier 2 predictors flagged for content overlap with frailty deficit items (8 direct and 21 proximal), leaving 132 Tier 2 predictors. The increment remained large, although attenuated (ΔR² = 29.5%).

The same Tier 2 block added little for epigenetic aging (ΔR² = 0.5%, n = 836), reducing concern that the increments reflect a generic modeling artifact. TabPFN, evaluated as a model-class benchmark, gave full-model R² within two percentage points of XGBoost for the three primary outcomes.
findings.read: Each bar is cross-validated R² for an age-adjusted outcome measured at Wave 1. The lighter segment is what the 16 background variables predict alone; the darker segment is what the Tier 2 block adds. Bracketed ranges are repeated cross-validation intervals: the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the increment over 15 repetitions with different fold assignments. They describe stability to the fold partition, not sampling error.
caveats: Frailty remains partly self-reported, so perceived control, negative affect, and related measures may covary with frailty through both substantive co-occurrence and shared reporting processes, even after excluding content-overlapping predictors.
The allostatic-load models kept twin participants in training. Holding every complete twin pair out (n = 1,403) gave a Tier 2 increment of 26.3%.
findings.source: Results, cross-sectional layer; SI Tables S2 and S18

findings.title: Measured at midlife, Tier 2 predictors also predict 9-year change in frailty and cognition
findings.lead: With the Wave 1 outcome and Tier 1 variables included, the Tier 2 block added reliably to the prediction of 9-year change for frailty and cognition. The allostatic-load increment was less stable.
body: Nine-year change is defined as the Wave 2 outcome conditional on its Wave 1 value. The Tier 2 block added ΔR² = 1.8% [repeated cross-validation interval: 1.3%, 2.2%] for frailty (n = 3,239) and 0.8% [0.5%, 1.0%] for cognition (n = 2,814). The allostatic-load increment was 1.1% [−0.4%, 3.4%] (n = 576), with an interval that included zero. Tier 1 variables themselves added 0.6%, 1.1%, and −0.7% beyond the Wave 1 outcome alone.

This scale is expected for change in health outcomes: baseline status already accounts for most of the predictable variance, so further information reflects differences in trajectories that baseline status does not capture. Judged against interpretable benchmarks rather than variance explained alone, increments of this size are a meaningful population-level contribution to the prediction of change, although not a basis for individual prediction.

A sensitivity analysis substituting Wave 2 predictors, still conditioning on the Wave 1 outcome, recovered more for frailty (1.8% to 9.6%) and allostatic load (1.1% to 4.8%) but little for cognition (0.8% to 1.2%). With the same Wave 2 predictors and no Wave 1 outcome, the increments were 35.1%, 9.8%, and 18.9%.

The two cohorts were followed over non-overlapping windows: the Refresher follow-up spans the COVID-19 pandemic, whereas the MIDUS 2 follow-up precedes it, so the pooled change increments average two periods, with the frailty increment arising mainly in MIDUS 2.
findings.read: Each bar is cross-validated R² for the Wave 2 outcome, built up from the Wave 1 outcome alone, then Tier 1, then Tier 2. The right-hand panel magnifies the Tier 2 increment with its repeated cross-validation interval. The concurrent and change increments differ in target, conditioning, and sample, so the site does not set them against each other as a ratio.
caveats: Conditioning on a baseline measured with error biases the increment. The Wave 2 predictor sensitivity analysis helps interpret the difference between concurrent and change increments but is itself exposed to reverse causation and time-varying confounding.
Longitudinal retention was 60.6% for frailty, 62.5% for cognition, and 32% for allostatic load, and completers were generally healthier or more cognitively advantaged at baseline (SI Table S11).
findings.source: Results, longitudinal layer; SI Fig. S1; SI Tables S11, S12 and S18

findings.title: Contributions are spread across many predictors, and leading predictors vary across resampled fits
findings.lead: Among the 161 Tier 2 predictors, 21 to 32 were needed to reach half of the total feature importance in the cross-sectional models, and 74 to 81 to reach 80 percent.
body: SHAP dependence plots characterize how each predictor relates to the model's predicted outcome across its observed range. Several model-implied patterns were nonlinear. Body mass index contributed to frailty and allostatic load in a threshold-like way, relatively flat below approximately 25 and rising between 28 and 35. Education, a Tier 1 variable, contributed most to predicted cognition, with stepwise gains at credential boundaries such as high-school completion and college degree; its mean |SHAP| was more than twice that of the next-ranked cognitive predictor. Sleep duration showed a U-shaped association with predicted frailty, near zero at 7 to 8 hours and higher at both shorter and longer durations.

Drinking status showed a non-monotonic pattern specific to allostatic load: past-month abstainers had the highest SHAP contributions, whereas current drinkers had lower ones. This pattern should be read as model-implied and specific to allostatic load, not as evidence that drinking is physiologically protective.

Feature-importance rankings were moderately correlated between the cross-sectional and 9-year change models (Spearman ρ = .70 to .80; top-20 overlap 10 to 12 of 19). Attribution was more widely distributed in the change models: 38 to 43 Tier 2 predictors were needed to reach half of the summed mean |SHAP|. The rankings were also unstable. Across the resampled fits of the change models, 111 distinct predictors for frailty, 114 for cognition, and 132 for allostatic load entered the top 20 at least once; only 10, 11, and 6 did so in at least 60 percent of fits.
findings.read: Mean |SHAP| is a predictor's average absolute contribution to the model's prediction, in the outcome's own age-adjusted units, so it ranks predictors within one outcome and model only. Whiskers are 95 percent intervals over the bootstrap fits; stability is the share of fits in which the predictor ranks in the top 20.
caveats: SHAP describes the fitted model, not a causal effect. Correlated predictors can share or trade attribution, which is one reason leading predictors vary across resampled fits.
findings.source: Results, cross-sectional and longitudinal layers; SI Figs S2 to S5; SI Table S17

findings.title: One outcome's top predictors recover part, but not all, of another outcome's prediction
findings.lead: Applying one outcome's top predictors to another recovered 25% to 73% of the target's own full-model R².
body: Splitting each outcome's top-20 predictors into those shared with another domain and those unique to it, target-unique predictors out-predicted shared ones in all 6 directed comparisons among the three domains.

Predictors recurring across outcomes were mixed rather than purely psychological: those appearing in four or more of the six top-20 lists included work status, work industry, occupational group, household income, received support, and waist-hip ratio. This set spans structural, resource-related, psychosocial, and body-composition markers and should be read as a recurring set rather than evidence for a single common cause. Beyond it, the most prominent predictors were psychological well-being and affect for frailty, education and cognitively engaging activities for cognition, and body composition and substance use for allostatic load.
findings.read: Each cell takes the 20 highest-ranked predictors of the row's outcome, fits a model for the column's outcome on them alone, and reports its cross-validated R² as a share of the column outcome's full-model R². The list below counts, for each recurring predictor, how many of the six outcome-by-layer top-20 lists (three outcomes, cross-sectional and change) it enters.
caveats: Recurrence of a predictor's identity is not transfer of predictive performance, and the data do not adjudicate between accounts of why structural and labor-market predictors recur.
findings.source: Results, cross-domain layer; SI Tables S3 and S17

findings.title: Within twin pairs, concurrent associations persist most broadly for frailty
findings.lead: Familial resemblance of concurrent aging status was moderate to high, and concurrent within-family associations were broadest for frailty, with limited evidence for associations with 9-year change.
body: Associations were decomposed into between-family and within-family components with mixed-effects models in the MIDUS twin subsample, held out from frailty and cognition training. To preserve power and limit multiple testing, the models were fitted to focal predictors rather than all 177: variables whose bootstrap top-20 membership in the corresponding predictive model was at least 60 percent, so the number tested differs by outcome and analysis. The pooled pairs are monozygotic (MZ), same-sex dizygotic, and opposite-sex dizygotic twins; no non-twin sibling pairs are included.

MZ intraclass correlations at Wave 1 were .37 for frailty, .62 for cognition, and .59 for allostatic load. For frailty, 12 within-family predictors survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction in all pairs, and 7 of these also survived in the MZ-only sensitivity analysis. For cognition, 4 survived in all pairs and none in the smaller MZ-only analysis. For allostatic load, BMI and life satisfaction survived in all pairs, and BMI alone in the MZ-only analysis.

For 9-year change, the twin sample was not powered for within-family inference: in all pairs, median minimum detectable effects were .16 to .29, roughly 60% to 91% of the median concurrent within-family association that survived FDR correction, and the only change association to survive was blue-collar occupational group with lower cognitive change.
findings.read: Each row is one focal predictor's within-pair association (βW, standardized by the within-pair standard deviations of predictor and outcome) with its 95 percent pair-bootstrap interval. Filled points survived FDR correction (q ≤ .05) within the outcome, pair sample, and analysis. The minimum detectable effect is the smallest standardized βW detectable with 80 percent power.
caveats: These analyses evaluate selected individual predictors, not the joint increments of the earlier layers. Within-family associations persist after shared family background is partially controlled, but they do not identify causal effects, since non-shared confounding, selection, and measurement error remain possible.
findings.source: Results, within-family layer; Table 1; SI Tables S4 to S10

findings.title: Favorable and unfavorable profiles of focal predictors shift model-predicted aging by bounded amounts
findings.lead: An exploratory, descriptive complement to the increments and the SHAP dependence results: how far each cross-sectional model's prediction moves across pre-specified favorable, neutral, and unfavorable settings of six focal predictors.
body: For frailty, the favorable profile predicted slightly lower frailty than the unfavorable profile (−0.085 versus −0.011; gap −0.073, 95% CI [−0.094, −0.053]). Its contrast is the narrowest of the three because its strongest cross-sectional predictors overlapped the frailty index and were excluded from its focal set.

For cognition, the favorable profile predicted substantially higher cognition (+0.837 versus −0.285; gap +1.122), dominated by education. For allostatic load, the favorable profile predicted lower load (−0.424 versus +0.263; gap −0.687), driven largely by BMI and waist-hip ratio.

Focal sets: frailty, perceived control over health, positive affect, life satisfaction, work status, perceived intellectual aging, and work industry; cognition, education, word games, computer use, occupational group, waist-hip ratio, and perceived intellectual aging; allostatic load, BMI, waist-hip ratio, drinking status, life satisfaction, work industry, and vigorous leisure activity. All other predictors are held at the sample reference.
findings.read: Points are model-predicted, age-residualized outcomes, where 0 is the sample average for a given age, with 95 percent bootstrap intervals. Labels give the sample percentile each prediction corresponds to. Outcomes are on their own scales.
caveats: The favorable-unfavorable contrast is an extreme joint-profile comparison, not a sum of causal effects. In the allostatic-load profiles, the unfavorable setting assigns past-month abstainer as the drinking category because the fitted model assigns abstainers the highest predicted load; this direction is confounded and is not a health recommendation.
findings.source: SI Appendix, Exploratory Profile Comparison; SI Fig. S7; SI Table S16

about.sample: MIDUS is a national longitudinal cohort of health and well-being across adulthood. Two cohorts were pooled: MIDUS 2 (baseline 2004-2009, follow-up 2013-2014) and the MIDUS Refresher (baseline 2011-2014, follow-up 2020-2022). The combined baseline sample included 6,651 participants, of whom 4,093 had follow-up data approximately nine years later. Outcome-specific samples were smaller because outcomes were measured in different MIDUS modules and waves.

outcomes.name: Frailty
outcomes.text: A 40-item deficit-accumulation index of physical limitations, chronic conditions, and related health deficits (38 items at the Refresher follow-up), with items flagged as psychological symptoms excluded to reduce predictor-outcome overlap.

outcomes.name: Cognition
outcomes.text: The composite score of the Brief Test of Adult Cognition by Telephone (BTACT), which captures episodic memory and executive function.

outcomes.name: Allostatic load
outcomes.text: A 16-biomarker composite spanning cardiovascular, metabolic, inflammatory, neuroendocrine, and renal systems. BMI and waist-hip ratio are retained as predictors rather than composite components.

outcomes.name: Epigenetic aging
outcomes.text: DNA-methylation PhenoAge, residualized, examined cross-sectionally only as a benchmark for the size of the Tier 2 increment.

about.predictors: Tier 1 comprises 16 demographic, early-life, family-history, and household-resource variables, held constant throughout. Tier 2 comprises 161 adult psychosocial and behavioral variables spanning personality, psychological well-being, social relationships, intimate partnership, mental health, coping, life evaluation, work and occupation, subjective socioeconomic resources, household context, health behaviors, cognitive activities, and substance use. The split is an analytic adjustment sequence rather than a claim that Tier 1 variables sit outside the broader social exposome: several Tier 2 subdomains, such as work, financial appraisal, and healthcare access, are themselves socioeconomic.
about.modeling: Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) are the primary model; TabPFN is a model-class benchmark. All R² values are out-of-fold under 5-fold cross-validation, with outcomes residualized on age within each fold. Hyperparameters were tuned within each fold, and feature importance was decomposed with TreeSHAP, with ranking stability assessed over 200 bootstrap fits. Participants from complete twin pairs were excluded from the frailty and cognition training samples and reserved for the within-family analyses; the allostatic-load models retained them, given the limited longitudinal biomarker sample.
limitations: The data are observational, and neither baseline adjustment nor within-family decomposition eliminates causal ambiguity.

Within-family estimates remain vulnerable to non-shared confounding, selection, measurement error, and, above all, limited power, particularly in the change models and especially for allostatic load and cognition.

MIDUS is predominantly non-Hispanic White and self-selected, so transportability across race, ethnicity, and less healthy populations is untested; these results describe this cohort rather than aging in general.
Cognition was assessed only by a brief telephone battery oriented to impairment, whose narrower measurable range in a non-demented sample may partly account for its weaker signal.
Single-occasion psychosocial measurement may miss within-person fluctuations detectable with denser sampling.
about.privacy: The site publishes aggregates only. Every SHAP bin, category level, and histogram bin covers at least ten people, and smoothed curves at least twenty. Continuous ranges are given as 1st and 99th percentiles, never observed extremes, and category levels held by fewer than ten people are not shown. MIDUS individual-level data are available from the MIDUS study, not from this site.

glossary.definition: R² is the share of variance in an outcome a model accounts for, estimated out of sample by cross-validation. ΔR² is the gain from adding the Tier 2 predictors to the model without them.

Tier 1 is the background block of demographic, early-life, family-history, and household-resource variables, held constant throughout. Tier 2 is the block of adult psychosocial and behavioral variables whose combined increment is tested.
Outcomes are residualized on age within each cross-validation fold, so 0 is the average for someone of the same age, and reported R² values are for age-adjusted outcomes.
The 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of an increment over 15 repetitions of 5-fold cross-validation with different fold assignments. It describes stability to the fold partition, not sampling error.

The Wave 2 outcome conditional on its Wave 1 value. Models include each person's Wave 1 value of the same outcome, so the Tier 2 increment is what the predictors add once current status is known. Two waves give a conditional change, not a rate.

SHapley Additive exPlanations assign each predictor a locally additive contribution to one prediction. Mean |SHAP|, the average absolute contribution across people, is the global importance statistic. SHAP describes the fitted model, not a causal effect.
The share of bootstrap refits in which a predictor ranks among the 20 most important. Focal predictors for the within-family models are those at or above 60 percent.
The association of a co-twin's deviation from the pair mean with the outcome, which holds family background shared by the pair partly constant.
False discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg), applied within each outcome, pair sample, and analysis rather than pooled across outcomes.
The smallest standardized within-pair association detectable with 80 percent power at two-sided α of five percent, a sensitivity analysis of power rather than power at the observed estimate.
